Surah 69: al-Haqqah (The Inevitable Reality). It is Meccan, and its verses number fifty-two.

﴿Al-Haqqah﴾: that is, the Hour (al-sa'ah), or the state that is certain to occur and bound to come without doubt; or the one in which the matters of reckoning, reward and punishment are realized as true (yahiqqu fīhā al-umūr al-haqqah min al-hisab wa-al-thawab wa-al-'iqab); or the one in which matters are verified, i.e., known in their reality, from haqqahu yahiqquhu, when one knows its reality. The verb is attributed to it figuratively (ja'ala al-fi'l laha wa-majazan), because of the matters that are in it, or because of the people of knowledge (ulu al-'ilm) who are in it. Whichever of these is the case, the omission of the qualified noun (hadhf al-mawsuf) serves to announce the complete manifestation of its being characterized by this attribute, and its functioning as a noun, and its being in the nominative as the predicate of the subject (al-ibtida'), its predicate being the following.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 2:

﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ (The commentator's view is that) "mā" is a second subject (mubtada'), and "al-ḥāqqah" is its predicate (khabar), and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject. The original form is "mā hiya", meaning: "what is it, in its state and its attributes?" For "mā" may be used to ask about attribute and state. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is for emphasis on its awesomeness. This is what they have mentioned in the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this clause and its counterparts. It has already been mentioned in the commentary on surah al-Waqi'ah that the requirement of precise verification (taḥqīq) is that the interrogative "mā" be the predicate of what follows it, since the essential point of the statement is to explain that the Inevitable Reality is a wondrous matter and a terrible affair, as is conveyed by "mā" being the predicate, not to explain that a wondrous matter is the Inevitable Reality, as would be conveyed by it being the subject and "al-ḥāqqah" being the predicate. And His saying, exalted is He:

{And what will make you know what the Reality is?} That is: what will inform you of what it is.

{What is the Reality?} This is an emphasis on its terror and dreadfulness, by explaining that it lies outside the sphere of knowledge of created beings, meaning that the greatness of its matter, the extent of its terror and its severity are such that the comprehension of no one barely reaches it, nor his imagination; and however you imagine its state, it is greater than that and greater still. Therefore the informing is not possible. What is in the position of nominative case is by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and "adraka" is its predicate. There is no room here for the reverse. "Ma al-Haqqah" is a sentence of subject and predicate; in the aspect you have come to know, its position is accusative by dropping the preposition, because adra (to know) transitively takes a second object with the preposition bi, as in His exalted saying: "wa la adrakum bihi" (and neither would He have informed you of it). So when the interrogative clause came as a suspension of it, it occupied the position of the second object. The great sentence is conjoined to what precedes it of the sentence that occurred as a predicate, by His exalted saying: "al-Haqqah" (the Reality), emphasizing its terror, as has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 4:

﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ That is, by the state that strikes people with various kinds of terror and dread, and by which the heaven is split asunder and cleft, the earth and the mountains are crushed and scattered, and the stars are obliterated and extinguished. Placing it in the position of the pronoun of al-Haqqah (the Inevitable Reality) serves to indicate the meaning of striking within it, in order to intensify its awfulness. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to inform him, upon him be prayers and peace, of some of the conditions of al-Haqqah, following the affirmation that no one informed him, upon him be prayers and peace, of what it is, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ ﴿A fierce Fire.﴾ Its parallels are similar, except that what is clarified there is the very thing asked about, whereas here it is one of its conditions, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.﴾ Just as what is clarified there is not the Night of Decree itself but its excellence and nobility, so too what is clarified here is the awfulness of al-Haqqah, the greatness of its matter, and that it is of such a nature that the destruction of whoever denies it is due. It is as if it were said: "And what will make you know what al-Haqqah is? Thamud and 'Ad denied it, so they were destroyed."
﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the overwhelming (blast)﴾. That is, by the calamity that exceeded all bounds, namely the Cry or the Quake.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 6:

﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious wind,﴾ meaning: intensely loud in its sound, having a roaring (ṣarṣara); or intensely cold, burning with its coldness.

﴿Violent (ʿātiya)﴾: intensely forceful in its blowing, as if it rebelled (ʿataw) against its keepers (khuzzān), so that they could not control it; or rebelled against ʿĀd, so that they could not repel it. And His, the Exalted's, statement:

﴿Sakhkharahā ʿalayhim﴾ ... etc. This is a *istinaf* (resumptive sentence, a new clause that begins a fresh point), introduced to explain how they were destroyed by the wind. That is: God gave it power over them by His overwhelming might.

﴿Seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾. *Ḥusūman* (حُسُومًا) means successive, plural of *ḥāsim* (حاسِم), like *shuhūd* (شُهُود), the plural of *shāhid*. It comes from *ḥasamtu al-dābba* (حَسَمْتُ الدّابَّةَ), meaning I cauterized the animal repeatedly. Alternatively, it means ill-omened days that wiped out every good and uprooted it, or days that cut off their last trace. *Ḥusūman* may also be a verbal noun in the accusative of purpose, meaning "for the purpose of cutting off," or a verbal noun in the accusative standing in place of an implied verb, meaning "they cut them off utterly" as a circumstantial clause. The reading with a *fatḥa* (the vowel-marked reading) supports this. These were the days of *al-ʿAjūz* (the Old Woman), from the morning of Wednesday to the sunset of the following Wednesday. They were called "the Old Woman" because an old woman of ʿĀd hid in a cave, and the wind seized her on the eighth day and destroyed her. It is also said that these were the days of *al-ʿAjz* (weakness), the last part of winter. Their names are al-Ṣinn, al-Ṣinnabr, al-Wabar, al-Āmir, al-Mu'tamar, al-Muʿallil, Muṭfi' al-Jamr, and, it is said, Mukfi' al-Ẓaʿn.

﴿Then you would see the people﴾, if you were present at that time.

﴿In it﴾: in its directions, or in those nights and days.

﴿Fallen﴾: dead, the plural of *ṣarīʿ* (صَرِيعٍ).

﴿As if they were trunks of palm trees﴾: that is, the roots of palm trees.

﴿Hollow﴾: whose insides had been eaten away.
﴿So do you see any remnant of them?﴾ That is: a remainder (baqiyah), or a surviving soul (nafs baqiyah), or survival (baqa'), taking it as a verbal noun (masdar) like "al-kadhibah" and "al-taghiyah."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 9:**

﴿And Pharaoh came, and those before him﴾: that is, those who preceded him. It is also read (*wa-min qablihi*), meaning: and those from among his followers who were with him; and what supports this is that it is read (*wa-man ma'ahu*), "and those who were with him."

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: that is, the towns of the people of Lut (Lot), meaning their inhabitants.

﴿With the sin﴾: with the wrongdoing, or with the deed, or with the deeds involving wrongdoing, among which is the denial of the Resurrection and the Last Day. (p-23)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 10:

﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾ i.e., every nation disobeyed its messenger when they forbade them from the vile deeds they were engaged in. ﴿So He seized them﴾ i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿With a severe seizing﴾ i.e., increased in severity, just as their vile deeds increased in vileness, from the root *riba* (to increase) of a thing when it grows.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed﴾ because of the persistence of the people of Noah in various kinds of disbelief and sins, and their exaggeration in denying him, upon him be prayer and peace, regarding what was revealed to him of the rulings, among which are the conditions of the Resurrection.

﴿We carried you﴾ i.e., in the loins of your fathers.

﴿in the sailing ship﴾ in the ship of Noah, upon him be peace. The meaning of their being carried in it is their being raised above the water until the end of the days of the Flood, not merely their being lifted into the ship, as the word "fi" (in) indicates. For it is not connected to the verb "carried," but is related to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its object, i.e., "We raised you above the water, and We preserved you while you were in the sailing ship, by Our command and Our protection." In this there is an indication that the basis of their salvation was purely God's protection, and that the ship was merely an apparent (ṣūrī) means.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 12:**

﴿So that We may make it﴾: i.e., so that We may make the act, which is an expression for the deliverance of the believers and the drowning of the disbelievers.

﴿A reminder for you﴾: a lesson and an indication of the perfect power of the Maker, His wisdom, the strength of His dominion, and the vastness of His mercy.

﴿And that a retaining ear may retain it﴾: i.e., preserve it. Wa'y (retention) means that you keep a thing in your own self, while iya' (storing) means that you keep it outside yourself in a receptacle (wi'a'). It is also read as ta'iyaha with the 'ayn pronounced with sukun, likening it to katif (shoulder). ﴿An ear that retains﴾: i.e., an ear whose nature is to preserve what must be preserved, by remembering it, spreading it, and reflecting upon it, and not wasting it by abandoning acting upon it. The indefinite form (tankir) indicates its scarcity, and that one whose condition is this, despite being rare, becomes the cause of the salvation of a vast multitude and the continuation of their offspring. It is also read ﴿udhnun﴾ with the letter being lightened.

Then, when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast, it begins to explain the Inevitable Reality (al-Ḥāqqah) itself and how it occurs, after explaining its great magnitude through the destruction of those who denied it. The verb was attributed to the verbal noun (maṣdar) "نَفْخَةٌ" (nafkhatun) in order to specify it, and its masculine form is appropriate because of the separation. It was also read as "نَفْخَةً واحِدَةً" (nafkhatan wāḥidatan) with the accusative, by attributing the verb to the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-l-majrūr). What is meant by it is the First Blast, at which the ruin of the world occurs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 14:

﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted up﴾, i.e., they are uprooted and raised from their places merely by the Divine power, or through the mediation of an earthquake or a violent wind.

﴿And they are crushed with one crushing﴾, i.e., the two (the earth and the mountains), after being raised, are struck against one another with a single blow, until they are broken apart and become a heap of sand poured out (kathiban mahilan) and scattered dust (habaan munbaththan). It was also said: they are spread out with a single spreading, so they become a level plain (qa'an safsafan), in which you see no crookedness or elevation, from their saying: indakka al-sanam (the hump [of the camel] became flattened), when it became level; a camel is adhdak and a she-camel is dakka'; and from it comes al-dukkan (the bench).

﴿So on that Day﴾: i.e., then, at that time.

﴿(p-24) the Inevitable Event occurred﴾: i.e., the Resurrection came to pass.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 16:**

﴿And the heaven will be split open﴾ because of the descent of the angels.

﴿So it﴾, that is, the heaven, ﴿on that Day will be frail﴾, weak and loose, after having been firmly constructed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 17:

﴿And the angels﴾, i.e., the creatures known as angels (malak).

﴿upon its edges﴾, i.e., its sides; plural of rajā (with a short vowel, rajā, "edge"), meaning: the sky, which is their dwelling, will split, and so they will take refuge at its sides and borders.

﴿And there will bear the Throne of your Lord above them﴾, above the angels who are the rajā'; or above the eight.

﴿On that Day, eight﴾ of the angels. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are now four, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah, exalted is He, will strengthen them with four others, so they will become eight. It is also related that they are eight angels whose feet are in the depths of the seventh earth, while the Throne is above their heads, and they are bowing their heads and glorifying (Allah). It has been said that some of them are in the form of a man, some in the form of a lion, some in the form of an ox, and some in the form of an eagle. It is also related that they are eight angels in the shape of mountain goats, the distance between whose hooves and knees is a journey of seventy years. And from Shahr ibn Hawshab: four of them say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your pardon after Your power," and four say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge." And from al-Hasan: "Allah knows best! Are they eight, or eight thousand?" And from al-Dahhak: "They are eight rows, the number of which none knows but Allah, exalted is He." It is possible that the eight are of the Spirit (al-Ruh), or of another creation. It has also been said that this is an illustration of His greatness, exalted is He, by what is witnessed of the conditions of kings on the day they come out before the people for a general judgment, since that is the utmost of what can be imagined of greatness and majesty; but His affairs, glory be to Him, are far more exalted than everything that the sphere of expression and allusion encompasses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 18:

﴿On that Day you will be exposed﴾ i.e., you will be questioned and called to account. He expressed it thus as a comparison to the sultan reviewing his troops (ʿarḍ al-sulṭān al-ʿaskar) in order to ascertain their conditions. It is related that on the Day of Resurrection there are three exposures (ʿurḍāt). As for two of them, they involve excuse-making, argumentation and reproach. As for the third, in it the books are unfolded (tunshar al-kutub), so the one who is successful takes his book in his right hand, and the one who is destroyed takes it in his left. And although this takes place after the second blast (al-nafkha al-thāniya), nevertheless, since "the day" (al-yawm) is a name for an extended period of time in which the two blasts, the swoon (al-ṣaʿqa), the resurrection (al-nushūr), the reckoning (al-ḥisāb), the entry of the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of Hellfire into Hellfire all occur, it is valid to make it a time-frame (ẓarf) for all of these.

﴿Not a thing concealed from you will be hidden﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject (marfūʿ) of "you will be exposed", i.e., you will be exposed while nothing of your secrets is hidden from Him, the Exalted, even before that; the exposure is only for the disclosure of the state and for emphasis on justice; or [it means] nothing will be hidden that day from people, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when the secrets will be tested﴾ [86:9]. It was also read as (yakhfā) with a yāʾ at the beginning (bi-l-yāʾ al-taḥtāniyya).

"Then as for him who is given his record in his right hand," — this is a detailed explanation of the rules of the presentation (al-'ard).

﴿So he will say﴾ — boastfully and joyfully.

﴿"Here, read my record!"﴾ — "Ha" is a name for "take" (khudh). It has three dialects, the best of which are: "hā'" for a masculine singular addressee, "hā'i" for a feminine singular addressee, "hāumā" for two men or two women, "hā'ūna" for men (plural), and "hā'unna" for women (plural). Its object is omitted. "Kitābiyah" is the object of "iqra'ū" (read), because it is the nearer of the two verbs; and because if it were the object of "hā'um" it would have been said "iqra'uhu," since the preferable course is to make the pronoun a suffix wherever possible. The "hā'" in it, and in "hisābiyah," "māliyah," and "sulṭāniyah," is the pause particle (al-sakt): it is written when stopping and dropped when continuing, and it is recommended to pronounce it because it is retained in the Imam (the master copy of the Qur'an).

Translation:

﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my reckoning.﴾ That is: I knew. Perhaps the expression of it by "ẓann" (supposition, assumption) is to indicate that what occurs to the soul of thoughts (khaṭarāt), which generally accompany theoretical knowledge (al-ʿulūm al-naẓariyyah) and from which they are not free, does not harm one's conviction (iʿtiqād).

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ — meaning one that is characterized by contentment (ذاتِ رِضًا), with the attribution made by way of the morphological form (ʿalā al-nisbah bi-l-ṣīghah), as one says "dāriʿ" (armored, i.e., possessing armor) with attribution by the letter (al-nisbah bi-l-ḥarf). Alternatively, the verb is ascribed to it metaphorically (majāzan), while it actually belongs to its possessor, namely because it is pure of impurities and lasting, joined with exaltation.

Fī jannatin ʿāliyah: "in a lofty garden" (ﷺ not applicable). Translating the passage:

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, high in place, because it is in the heaven, or in its ranks (of degrees), or in its buildings and trees.

**﴿Qutufuha﴾** (its clusters/fruits) is the plural of **qiṭf** (qiṭf: that which is picked quickly), and **al-qatf** (with a fatḥah) is a verbal noun (maṣdar).

**﴿Dāniyah﴾** (near, within reach): one who is seated can reach it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 24:

﴿Eat and drink﴾, with the verb of saying (qawl) implied; the plural is used in view of the meaning.

﴿with relish﴾: eating and drinking with relish (hani'an), or "may you be given it with relish" (hunnitum hani'an).

﴿for what you sent forward﴾: with what precedes it, namely the righteous deeds that you sent ahead.

﴿in the days that are past﴾: that is, the days that passed in the world. From Mujahid: the days of fasting. It is also narrated that Allah the Exalted says: "O My friends, I have long looked upon you in the world, while your lips were dried from drinks, your eyes were sunken, and your bellies were emptied; so be now in your bliss, and ﴿eat and drink﴾," (the verse).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 25:

﴿And as for him who is given his record in his left hand﴾, and he is shown what is in it of ugly deeds, ﴿so he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!"﴾.

Verse 26 of Surah al-Haqqah (69): ﴿And I did not know what my reckoning was﴾.

He says this because of what he witnessed of the evil outcome.

Qur'an 69:27: "Would that it had been the decisive death!"

Here the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) explains: ﴿Would that it were⦆ — would that the death I died ﴿had been the decisive one⦆. That is, the one that cut off my affair: I would not have been raised after it, and would not have met what I have met. So the pronoun in "would that it" (yalaytaha) refers to "the death" (al-mawtah).

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the state he witnessed: would that this state had been the death that finished me off, because he found it more bitter than death, and so he wished for death in its presence. It has also been allowed that the pronoun refers to the worldly life, i.e. (p-26) would that the worldly life had been (only) the death, and that I had not been created alive.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿What has my wealth availed me?﴾ — that is, what of my wealth and my followers (did they avail me)? This is on the reading that "mā" is a negative particle and the object is omitted; or it is an interrogative "mā" expressing denial, meaning: "What benefit did what I had of affluence bring me?"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 29:

﴿My authority has perished from me.﴾ That is: my dominion and my power over people; or my proof which I used to argue with in the world; or my power over the faculties and the instruments, so that I became unable to employ them in acts of worship.
﴿Seize him﴾ is a narration of what Allah the Exalted says on that Day to the guardians of the Fire (khazanah al-nar): ﴿then shackle him﴾, meaning fasten him with chains (aghlal).

Then cast him into the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim) [lit. "then the hellfire, cast him into it"].

Note: the passage above is a direct translation of the given text as requested; here is the full rendering:

"Then the Jahim (Blazing Fire): cast him into it." That is, do not cause him to burn except in al-Jahim, which is the great Fire, so that the recompense accords with the disobedience, since he used to act arrogantly toward people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 32:

﴿Then in a chain whose length is seventy cubits﴾ That is: its length. ﴿Then thread him onto it﴾ i.e., insert him into it, by winding it around his body, so that he is within it, bound, unable to move at all. The mention of the chain first is like the mention of the Blazing Fire (al-jaḥīm) first, to indicate specificity and concern with mentioning the kinds of punishment by which he is tormented. And "then" (thumma) indicates the difference between the shackling (al-ghall), the burning (al-taṣliyah), and what lies between them, and between threading him in the chain in terms of severity.

Verse 33 of Surah 69: "Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty."

Translation of the commentary:

﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty﴾ is a justification given by way of a confirmatory resumptive clause (al-isti'naf al-tahqiqi). The description of Him, exalted is He, as "the Mighty" serves to make known that He alone deserves greatness, so whoever ascribes greatness to himself deserves the most severe punishments.

ولا يَحُضُّ عَلى طَعامِ المِسْكِينِ — "and does not urge the feeding of the poor." That is, he does not urge the giving of his food, or urge feeding [the poor] at all, let alone give out some of his own wealth. It was said: the urging is mentioned as a warning that one who does not urge [others] to this is in such a state, so what do you suppose of one who abandons the act itself. In it there is evidence that the disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary (furu') commandments as regards liability to punishment. They said: the two matters are singled out for mention because the most abominable of beliefs is disbelief (kufr), and the most hideous of vices is stinginess (bukhl) and hardness of heart.
So he will have no close friend here today who would protect him, ward off (punishment) from him, and grieve for him; for his allies will shun him and flee from him.

Quran 69:36: "Nor any food except from ghislin" — that is, from the washings of the people of the Fire and their pus; it is of the form fi'lin from al-ghasl (washing).

Translation of the passage:

﴿وَلا طَعامٌ إلا مِن غِسْلِينٍ﴾ "Nor any food except from ghislin" — that is, from the wash-water (ghusala) of the people of the Fire and their pus (sadid), (p-27) it being of the pattern fi'lin, derived from al-ghasl (washing).

"None eats it except the sinners (al-khati'un)": the people of sins, from the verb khati'a (خَطِئَ) when a man deliberately commits a sin, not from khata' (خَطَأ) in the sense opposed to correctness (sawab), nor in the sense opposed to intention (al-'amd).

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are the polytheists (al-mushrikun).

It is also read as (al-khatiyun), with the hamza replaced by a ya', and it is read with the hamza dropped. It has also been permitted that by them is meant those who overstep the truth toward falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah.

﴿So I swear﴾, meaning: "fa- uqsimu," on the basis that "lā" is a superfluous particle (mazīdah) used for emphasis (ta'kīd). As for interpreting it to mean the negation of swearing, on the grounds that the matter is manifest and needs no confirmation, this is refuted by the specification of what is sworn by, in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿by what you see﴾.

﴿And what you do not see﴾, as has passed in Surat al-Waqi'ah (Surah 56). That is: I swear by what is witnessed and what is unseen. It has been said: by this world and the Hereafter; it has been said: by bodies and spirits, by humankind and jinn, by creation and the Creator, and by the apparent and hidden blessings. The first (view) encompasses all of them.

ī﴿إنَّهُ﴾ That is: the Qur'an.

﴿لَقَوْلُ رَسُولٍ﴾ It is the word of a messenger who conveys it from God, exalted is He; for the messenger does not speak from himself. ﴿كَرِيمٍ﴾ Noble in the sight of God, exalted is He. This is the Prophet (ﷺ), or Jibril (peace be upon them both).

﴿And it is not the word of a poet﴾, as you claim at times.

﴿Little do you believe﴾, that is, you believe, but only a little.

Translation of the passage:

﴿Nor is it the word of a soothsayer﴾ — as you claim it to be, on another occasion.

﴿Little do you remember﴾ — that is, a little remembrance, or a short time in which you remember. The "little" is taken to mean negation, i.e., you neither believe nor remember at all. It has been said: faith was mentioned together with the denial of poetry, and remembrance together with the denial of soothsaying, because the fact that the Qur'an does not resemble poetry is a clear matter which none denies except a stubborn opponent, unlike its distinction from soothsaying. For soothsaying depends on recalling his circumstances, peace be upon him, and the meanings of the Qur'an that contradict the methods of soothsayers and the content of their statements. You know well that this too does not depend on reflection in any certain way. It is also read with the letter yā' (ي) in both places.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 43:

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ He sent it down upon the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 44:

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ Fabrication (al-iftira') is called taqawwul (fabricating speech), because it is speech that is forced and contrived. The fabricated sayings are called aqawil (sayings) in order to belittle them, as though it were the plural of uf'ula from qawl (speech), like al-adahik (the jesters' jokes).
(p-28) ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ — i.e., by his right hand.

﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾, i.e., the veins (niyat, sing. niyat) of his heart, by striking his neck. This is a depiction of his destruction by the most atrocious means that kings employ against those with whom they are angry: that the executioner (al-qattal) seizes him by his right hand, throws him down (yakfahuhu) with the sword, and strikes his neck. It was also said: "al-yamin" (the right hand) here means strength. One of them said:

Whenever a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah meets it with the right hand (al-yamin).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 47:

﴿So none of you﴾, O people,

﴿could withhold [Us] from him﴾, from the killing or from the one killed,

﴿[any] one who would prevent [it]﴾, preventing [it]. It is a qualifier of "one" (aḥad), since the latter is general in meaning.

"And indeed it" — i.e., and indeed the Qur'an.

"It is surely a reminder for the God-conscious (al-muttaqin)" — because they are the ones who benefit from it.
﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers﴾, so that We may requite them for their denial.
Verse 50 of Surah al-Haqqah: ﴿And indeed it is a cause of regret for the disbelievers﴾, at the time they witness the reward of the believers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 51:

﴿And indeed it is the absolute truth of certainty.﴾ The one around which no doubt whatsoever hovers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 69, verse 52:

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ That is: glorify by mentioning His great name, declaring Him far above being pleased with fabrication against Him, and giving thanks for what has been revealed to you.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Haqqah, Allah will reckon with him a light reckoning."
